title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 10: Ready for the Bio-Age
keywords: the very essence of life itself
PhilJA Chancellor Ameurfina A. Melencio Herrera
primary_topics: Chapter 10 of 'A Centenary of Justice' -- CJP's plenary remarks (July 1, 2001) at the Einstein Institute (Einshac) 'Working Conversation' on biosciences and biotechnology in Kona, Hawaii, assessing the Philippine judiciary's readiness for the 'bio-age'

The new-paradigm landscape facing the world's judiciaries: economic globalization/deregulation/privatization breaking down sovereign borders, the information highway transforming wealth, and -- most daunting -- genomics, genetic engineering and biotechnology reshaping 'the very essence of life itself' and the ways of 'discovering and processing truth'

The founding and meaning of judicial independence: the SC reckoned from 1901 (Second Philippine Commission, after the 1898 Treaty of Paris) because that is when an independent tribunal arose; independence defined as non-reviewable decisions, constitutionally guaranteed funding, and security of tenure (to age 70) and compensation

The five powers of the Supreme Court and how each equips it for biosciences: ordinary review; extraordinary certiorari review for grave abuse; administrative supervision and discipline of courts; control of admission to the bar; and rule-making -- closing on DNA exonerations and CJP's principled opposition to the death penalty
sub_topics: The setting: a judicial scholarship to the Einshac 'Working Conversation' in Kona, Hawaii (June 30-July 4, 2001), attended with Justice Leonardo A. Quisumbing and PhilJA Chancellor Ameurfina A. Melencio Herrera, gathering ~100 leaders of law and science to assess judiciaries' readiness for DNA, cloning, stem cells and genetic engineering

Justice Claire L'Heureux-Dube (Canadian Supreme Court) on judicial and constitutional globalization, illustrated by 'the Harvard mouse and Monsanto's canola'; Judge Clifford Wallace (US Court of Appeals; consultant to 40+ judiciaries) as a co-panelist

The economic and informational paradigms: deregulation, liberalization and privatization shrinking the world into a 'borderless global village' under the WTO; the shift 'from the manufacture and sale of products to the rendering of services, and from the exploitation of natural resources to the exploration and use of knowledge'

The bioscience challenge as 'the most daunting' -- genomics, genetic engineering and biotechnology affecting health, longevity, ethics, morality and 'the very essence of life,' causing 'mega-shifts in the ways of discovering and processing truth'

The founding rationale restated internationally: although Spanish- and US-military courts existed for almost 400 years, the SC is reckoned from 1901 because only then was a tribunal enjoying judicial independence set up; decisions were appealable to the US Supreme Court until 1946

The meaning of 'independent': (1) decisions not reviewable by any other government agency; (2) constitutionally guaranteed financial stability (Congress cannot reduce judicial appropriations below the previous year); (3) security of tenure (to age 70) and of compensation, with removal of SC justices only by impeachment

The five powers of the Supreme Court: (1) ordinary review of appeals; (2) extraordinary certiorari review of any agency -- including the Presidency and Congress -- for grave abuse of discretion (constitutional/legal/doctrinal violation, or whimsical, biased action denying due process); (3) administrative supervision and sole power to discipline and dismiss judges; (4) control of admission to and discipline of the bar; (5) preparation of rules of procedure and evidence

How each power meets biosciences: certiorari/review over the DOH, DA, Bureau of Patents and FDA, and power to void laws on abortion, cloning, genetic testing and privacy; rule-making on DNA fingerprinting, genes as evidence and electronic evidence; bar/curriculum and PhilJA continuing education; uniform ethical/doctrinal application through discipline; and -- via independence -- the capacity to enter international judicial agreements without other-branch approval

Epilogue on truth and the death penalty: Time magazine (Nov 13, 2000) reported 80 US convicts later exonerated by DNA; CJP 'shudders' that Philippine trial courts imposed death on more than 1,500 persons in five years -- 'a penalty which, incidentally, I personally oppose on constitutional and philosophical grounds' -- concluding that scientific breakthroughs can minimize 'mistakes in the discovery of truth'

stances.claim: The Philippine judiciary is structurally ready for the bio-age: its five constitutional powers -- ordinary and certiorari (grave-abuse) review, administrative supervision and discipline, control of the bar, and rule-making -- let it pass upon science/health agencies, void laws on cloning, genetic testing and privacy, promulgate rules on DNA and genetic evidence, shape legal curricula, ensure uniform ethical application, and (because it is independent) enter international judicial agreements without any other branch's approval.
stances.rhetorical_move: powers-map-to-challenges: demonstrating institutional readiness by matching each enumerated constitutional power to a specific bioscience problem
stances.confidence: asserted as a confident assessment of Philippine judicial preparedness

stances.claim: New scientific tools for 'discovering truth' reinforce the case against capital punishment: with 80 US convicts exonerated by later DNA evidence, and Philippine trial courts having imposed death on more than 1,500 persons in five years, CJP reiterates that he 'personally oppose[s]' the death penalty 'on constitutional and philosophical grounds,' because executions make errors irreversible while science can increasingly prevent them.
stances.rhetorical_move: science-against-irreversibility: enlisting DNA exoneration data to buttress a constitutional/philosophical objection to an irreversible penalty
stances.confidence: openly stated as CJP's personal and principled position

notable_anecdotes: The Hawaii scholarship: CJP attended the Einshac 'Working Conversation' in Kona, Hawaii (June 30-July 4, 2001) on a judicial scholarship alongside Justice Leonardo A. Quisumbing and PhilJA Chancellor Ameurfina A. Melencio Herrera -- an encounter of ~100 leaders of law and science he frames as ushering 'the bio-age into the Philippine judiciary' during its centenary.

The Harvard mouse and Monsanto canola: Canadian Justice Claire L'Heureux-Dube illustrated judicial globalization with two concrete biotech cases -- the patentable 'Harvard mouse' and Monsanto's genetically engineered canola.

Appealable to Washington until 1946: CJP notes that Philippine Supreme Court decisions remained appealable to the US Supreme Court until 1946, 'when the US completely withdrew its sovereign claims over our country' -- a marker of when full independence arrived.

The 80 exonerations: citing Time (Nov 13, 2000) that 80 US convicts by final judgment were later exonerated by DNA, CJP says he 'shudder[s]' that Philippine trial courts had imposed death on more than 1,500 persons in five years -- a penalty he opposes 'on constitutional and philosophical grounds.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces CJP's plenary remarks of July 1, 2001 at the Einstein Institute (Einshac) 'Working Conversation' on biosciences and biotechnology in Kona, Hawaii -- a conference of about 100 leaders of law and science he attended on a judicial scholarship with Justice Leonardo A. Quisumbing and PhilJA Chancellor Ameurfina A. Melencio Herrera, framing it as ushering 'the bio-age into the Philippine judiciary' during its centenary. Building on Canadian Justice Claire L'Heureux-Dube's account of judicial and constitutional globalization (with her 'Harvard mouse and Monsanto's canola' examples), he surveys the new paradigms confronting the world's courts: economic deregulation, liberalization and privatization dissolving sovereign borders under the WTO; the information highway shifting wealth 'from the exploitation of natural resources to the exploration and use of knowledge'; and -- 'most daunting' -- genomics, genetic engineering and biotechnology reshaping health, ethics and 'the very essence of life itself.' Answering for the Philippines, he restates that the SC is reckoned from 1901 (after the 1898 Treaty of Paris) because only then did an independent tribunal arise, with decisions appealable to the US Supreme Court until 1946, and defines judicial independence as non-reviewable decisions, constitutionally guaranteed funding, and security of tenure (to age 70) and compensation. He then enumerates the Court's five powers -- ordinary review; certiorari review of any agency, including the Presidency and Congress, for grave abuse of discretion; administrative supervision and discipline of judges; control of the bar; and rule-making -- and maps each to bioscience readiness: reviewing the DOH, DA, Bureau of Patents and FDA, voiding laws on cloning, genetic testing and privacy, promulgating rules on DNA and electronic evidence, shaping curricula through bar exams and PhilJA, ensuring uniform ethical application, and entering international judicial agreements unaided. He closes on truth: Time magazine's report that 80 US convicts were later exonerated by DNA leads him to 'shudder' that Philippine trial courts had imposed death on more than 1,500 persons in five years -- 'a penalty which, incidentally, I personally oppose on constitutional and philosophical grounds' -- concluding that scientific breakthroughs can ensure 'mistakes in the discovery of truth can be minimized, if not totally avoided.'
